title: Findings
text: A results overview for the two-study eye-tracking investigation of processing fluency in intuitive semantic-coherence judgments (Dyads-of-Triads task). Study 1 manipulates the emotional valence of the solvable triad (a semantic fluency source); Study 2 crosses valence with visual contrast (a perceptual fluency source). Outcomes: accuracy, response time, confidence, and gaze preference. Analysed samples: N = 39 (Study 1), N = 45 (Study 2). Full detail is in the per-study analysis pages linked in the navigation bar; per-condition estimates are in the deposited output/ tables.

title: Findings
text:
1 Headline
Objective accuracy is stable at ceiling and unmoved by either manipulation, while subjective experience is not: affective fluency (positive valence) speeds responses and raises confidence, whereas perceptual fluency (visual contrast) moves neither. Fluency sources therefore do not translate equivalently into metacognitive experience — the affective quality of a source, not processing ease alone, drives its effect on intuitive judgment.

title: Findings
text:
2 Study 1 — emotional valence

Accuracy (H1). At ceiling in every condition (Negative .90, Neutral .94, Positive .92; all above chance p < .001) and unaffected by valence, χ²(2) = 1.63, p = .443. The null is constrained by the ceiling.
Response time (H2). Valence sped responses, χ²(2) = 17.96, p < .001: positive-solution triads were fastest, faster than negative (c = 0.10, p = .001, d = 0.38) and neutral (c = 0.12, p < .001, d = 0.45); negative vs. neutral did not differ.
Confidence (H3). Valence raised confidence, χ²(2) = 13.70, p = .001: positive highest (M = 8.25) vs. negative (7.60; d = 0.34) and neutral (7.49; d = 0.39).
Gaze preference (H4). A growth-curve analysis showed a valence main effect, χ²(2) = 7.58, p = .023, and valence × time interactions across all polynomial terms (p < .001): valence modulates the time course of the bias toward the solvable triad. Overall pairwise differences between conditions were not significant.
Inspection time. Longer inspection of the solvable triad went with lower confidence (repeated-measures r = −.18, p < .001), consistent with a decision-difficulty account; it did not predict accuracy.

title: Findings
text:
3 Study 2 — valence × contrast

Accuracy (H1). Again at ceiling (all conditions > 86%, above chance p < .001); no effect of valence, contrast, or their interaction.
Response time (H2). No effect of valence (χ²(2) = 2.71, p = .258), contrast (χ²(3) = 1.43, p = .698), or their interaction (χ²(6) = 10.94, p = .090).
Confidence (H3). Valence again raised confidence — a main effect, χ²(2) = 18.02, p < .001, partially replicating Study 1 — while contrast and the interaction did not.
Gaze preference (H4). Both factors modulated gaze, with a valence × contrast interaction (all χ² p < .001): perceptual salience shifted overt attention even though it did not move the metacognitive measures — a dissociation between attentional capture and the felt sense of coherence.
Inspection time. As in Study 1, longer inspection went with lower confidence (r = −.27, p < .001).

title: Findings
text:
4 Robustness and boundary conditions

Evidence for the contrast nulls. Equivalence tests (TOST, SESOI d = 0.46) find the contrast effect statistically equivalent to zero for all response-time contrasts and for five of six confidence contrasts (none–both marginal, p = .051) — pointing to an absence of contrast effects. Simulation-based power shows the Study 2 contrast analyses were only modestly powered (37.5–49% at the SESOI), so the nulls are interpreted cautiously.
Cross-study divergence. The valence effect on response time differs between studies (valence × study interaction, χ²(2) = 7.66, p = .022); a dispersion model does not support the contrast manipulation inflating response-time variance (p = .69).
Stimulus confounds. Controlling simultaneously for frequency, length, arousal, and imageability (SUBTLEX-PL; ANPW_R), the valence effects remain significant but attenuated — Study 1 response time χ²(2) = 23.05 → 11.77 (p = .003), confidence χ²(2) = 15.40 → 6.69 (p = .035); Study 2 confidence χ²(2) = 17.24 → 6.58 (p = .037).
Item-level caveat. With five (Study 1) or six (Study 2) triads per condition, valence cannot be fully separated from unmeasured item idiosyncrasy; larger stimulus sets would be needed to resolve this. The effects are robust to the measured item properties above.

title: Findings
text:
5 Interpretation
Intuitive coherence judgment separates into a stable detection process (accuracy) and a malleable metacognitive evaluation (response time, confidence, gaze). Affective fluency shapes the latter; perceptual fluency does not — challenging the assumption that any source of processing ease yields an equivalent metacognitive signal, and pointing to the felt, affective quality of fluency as the active ingredient.

title: Robustness and supplementary analyses
text:
1 Overview
This notebook collects robustness and supplementary analyses that sit on top of the per-study results: (1) stimulus norming and the covariate confound test, (2) a sex-moderation check, (3) the cross-study reaction-time comparison, (4) equivalence tests for the Study 2 null effects, and (5) simulation-based power. The heavier computations live in standalone scripts (scripts/build_norms.R, scripts/power_simulation.R) whose cached outputs are read here.


2 Stimulus norming and the covariate confound test
Triad words were matched to Polish norms — ANPW_R (Imbir, 2016: valence, arousal, imageability, concreteness) and SUBTLEX-PL (Mandera et al., 2015: frequency, length) — by scripts/build_norms.R. ANPW_R is a general 4,905-word list (not restricted to affective words), so its affective ratings cover most triad words; the affective dimensions are available for 14/15 (Study 1) and 17/18 (Study 2) solvable triads, spread evenly across valence conditions.


Code

# Do the lexical/affective properties differ across valence conditions? Tested within each study

Within each study, the conditions did not differ significantly on any measured property (all p > .12), though these between-item comparisons are underpowered at five to six triads per condition; frequency and length nonetheless vary numerically across conditions. The key test is whether the affect effects survive controlling for these properties. We fit one covariate model per outcome: an affect-only base and an adjusted model adding frequency, length, arousal, and imageability, both on the same covariate-complete triads, so the before/after comparison is like-for-like.


Code
covariates <- c("frequency", "length", "arousal", "imageability")

# Base and adjusted models use the same complete-case rows.
covariate_test <- function(study, e, dv) {
  d <- trial_rt(e) %>% left_join(props, by = "triad_solvable")
  d$y <- if (dv == "rt") log(d$rt) else d$confidence
  d <- d %>% filter(!is.na(y), if_all(all_of(covariates), \(x) !is.na(x)))
  rhs <- paste(sprintf("scale(%s)", covariates), collapse = " + ")
  base <- glmmTMB(y ~ affect + (1 | participant_id) + (1 | trial), d)
  cov  <- glmmTMB(as.formula(paste("y ~ affect +", rhs, "+ (1 | participant_id) + (1 | trial)")), d)
  a0 <- car::Anova(base); a1 <- car::Anova(cov)
  tibble(study = study, outcome = dv,
         n_triads = n_distinct(d$triad_solvable), n_trials = nrow(d),
         chisq_base = a0[rownames(a0) == "affect", "Chisq"],
         p_base     = a0[rownames(a0) == "affect", "Pr(>Chisq)"],
         chisq_cov  = a1[rownames(a1) == "affect", "Chisq"],
         p_cov      = a1[rownames(a1) == "affect", "Pr(>Chisq)"])
}
cov_results <- bind_rows(
  covariate_test("Study 1", e1, "rt"),
  covariate_test("Study 1", e1, "confidence"),
  covariate_test("Study 2", e2, "confidence")
)
write_csv(cov_results, here("output/tables/covariate_tests.csv"))

The affect effect on response time and confidence remained significant after adjustment, though attenuated (the omnibus χ² roughly halves) — reduced but not explained by the measured lexical and affective properties. Two qualifications: with only five to six triads per condition the affect effect cannot be fully separated from unmeasured item idiosyncrasy — resolving that would require more triads per condition than this stimulus set provides — and triad-level affective values are means over each triad’s ANPW_R-covered words. (Study 2’s affect effect is tested here pooling over contrast, which is randomised over triads and orthogonal to valence by design.)


3 Sex moderation
We probed whether participant sex moderates the effects by adding sex and its interactions with the manipulations to the behavioural models (accuracy, reaction time, confidence). Male participants are few (Study 1 n = 11; Study 2 n = 6), so these tests are underpowered; a full sex × affect × contrast model for Study 2 is singular, so sex is crossed with each manipulation separately.


Code
sex_behav <- function(e, extra = character()) e %>%
  group_by(across(all_of(c("participant_id", "sex", "affect", extra, "trial")))) %>%
  summarise(accuracy = first(accuracy), rt = first(accuracy_rt), confidence = first(confidence), .groups = "drop")
b1 <- sex_behav(e1); b2 <- sex_behav(e2, "contrast")

sex_term <- function(d, dv, rhs, study) {
  d <- d %>% filter(!is.na(.data[[dv]]), !is.na(sex))
  d$y <- if (dv == "rt") log(d[[dv]]) else d[[dv]]
  m <- glmmTMB(as.formula(paste("y ~", rhs, "+ (1 | participant_id) + (1 | trial)")), d,
               family = if (dv == "accuracy") binomial() else gaussian())
  a <- car::Anova(m, type = 2)
  keep <- grepl("sex", rownames(a)) & grepl(":", rownames(a))
  tibble(study = study, outcome = dv, term = rownames(a)[keep],
         chisq = a[keep, "Chisq"], df = a[keep, "Df"], p_value = a[keep, "Pr(>Chisq)"])
}
sex_results <- bind_rows(
  map_dfr(c("accuracy", "rt", "confidence"), \(dv) sex_term(b1, dv, "affect * sex", "Study 1")),
  map_dfr(c("accuracy", "rt", "confidence"), \(dv) sex_term(b2, dv, "affect * sex", "Study 2")),
  map_dfr(c("accuracy", "rt", "confidence"), \(dv) sex_term(b2, dv, "contrast * sex", "Study 2"))
)

# Does the contrast manipulation inflate residual RT variance within Study 2?
rt2 <- e2 %>% group_by(participant_id, affect, contrast, trial) %>%
  summarise(log_rt = log(first(accuracy_rt)), .groups = "drop") %>% filter(is.finite(log_rt))
disp <- anova(glmmTMB(log_rt ~ affect * contrast + (1 | participant_id) + (1 | trial), rt2),
              glmmTMB(log_rt ~ affect * contrast + (1 | participant_id) + (1 | trial), dispformula = ~ contrast, rt2))

The affect × study interaction is significant — the valence effect on reaction time genuinely differs between studies. The dispersion model, however, shows the contrast manipulation did not significantly inflate reaction-time variance (LRT p = 0.69), so an “added variability” account of the divergence is not supported and is best treated as speculative.


5 Equivalence tests for the Study 2 null effects


Code
equiv <- function(dv) {
  d <- e2 %>% group_by(participant_id, affect, contrast, trial) %>%
    summarise(y = first(if (dv == "rt") log(accuracy_rt) else confidence), .groups = "drop") %>% filter(!is.na(y))
  m <- glmmTMB(y ~ affect * contrast + (1 | participant_id) + (1 | trial), d)
  delta <- sesoi_d * sigma(m)                                  # SESOI in raw units
  emm <- emmeans(m, ~ contrast)
  test(contrast(emm, "pairwise"), delta = delta, side = "equivalence") %>%
    as.data.frame() %>% mutate(outcome = dv, delta = round(delta, 3))
}
equiv_results <- bind_rows(equiv("rt"), equiv("confidence"))
write_csv(equiv_results, here("output/tables/equivalence_tests.csv"))

  group_by(affect) %>%

title: Preprocessing — Dyads-of-Triads fluency eye-tracking
text:
1 Overview
This notebook turns the extractor’s outputs into the analysis-ready eye-tracking datasets used by the Study 1 and Study 2 notebooks. The raw eye-tracking (.hdf5) and behavioral (.csv) records are first combined into per-sample tables by scripts/extract_data.py; here we add gaze quality control, areas of interest, and the response-window subset.

Inputs: data/processed/labelled/exp{1,2}.csv (gaze samples) and …/behavioral/exp{1,2}.csv (per-trial behavior), plus …/stimuli.csv.
Outputs: data/processed/prepared/exp{1,2}.Rds — an eyetrackingR object per study.

The pipeline, per study:

Combine gaze with behavior on (participant, trial, event), keeping each participant’s last run.
Binocular gaze: average the two eyes when both are valid, fall back to the single valid eye, and flag track loss otherwise — an eye is valid when its coordinates fall within the screen (± a 10% margin).
Interpolate gaps in gaze coordinates up to 100 ms; longer gaps stay track loss.
Remove outliers: reaction times beyond 1.5 × IQR (per participant) and gaze coordinates beyond the 97.5th Mahalanobis percentile (per trial).
Assign AOIs for the solvable and nonsolvable triads, restrict to the 10 s response window, and exclude trials/participants with more than 40% track loss.







NoteGaze quality control



Gaze validity uses a coordinate-plausibility check (samples with implausible off-screen coordinates are flagged as track loss) with a best-available-eye fallback; short gaps in the gaze coordinates are interpolated (capped at 100 ms) and longer gaps are left as track loss.




Code
prepare_experiment <- function(name, n_trials, has_contrast) {
  ct <- cols(participant_id = col_character(), .default = col_guess())
  gaze <- read_csv(here("data/processed/labelled", paste0(name, ".csv")), col_types = ct)
  beh  <- read_csv(here("data/processed/behavioral", paste0(name, ".csv")), col_types = ct)

  combined <- combine_gaze_behavioral(gaze, beh, n_trials)
  n_joined <- n_distinct(combined$participant_id)

  # Binocular gaze (best-available eye) in screen pixels, with a track-loss flag.
  xy <- compute_binocular_gaze(combined$left_gaze_x, combined$left_gaze_y,
                               combined$right_gaze_x, combined$right_gaze_y,
                               screen_width, screen_height, gaze_margin)
  combined <- combined %>%
    bind_cols(xy) %>%
    mutate(
      affect = factor(affect, levels = affect_levels),
      sex    = factor(case_when(sex == "k" ~ "Female", sex == "m" ~ "Male", TRUE ~ "Other")),
      Target = side_solve
    )
  if (has_contrast) {
    # Contrast condition, relative to the solvable triad (black = high contrast).
    combined <- combined %>%
      mutate(contrast = factor(case_when(
        side_contrast == "Both"        ~ "Both",
        side_contrast == "Neither"     ~ "None",
        side_contrast == side_solve    ~ "Solvable",
        TRUE                           ~ "Nonsolvable"
      ), levels = contrast_levels))
  }

  # Time from trial onset (s) + capped interpolation of gaze within each trial.
  combined <- combined %>%
    group_by(participant_id, trial) %>%
    mutate(
      time_from_onset = time - min(time),
      gaze_x = interpolate_coordinate(gaze_x, time_from_onset, max_gap_s),
      gaze_y = interpolate_coordinate(gaze_y, time_from_onset, max_gap_s),
      trackloss = is.na(gaze_x) | is.na(gaze_y)
    ) %>%
    ungroup()

  # Remove RT outliers (per participant) and gaze-coordinate outliers (per trial).
  combined <- combined %>%
    group_by(participant_id) %>%
    mutate(rt_outlier = identify_rt_outliers(accuracy_rt, trial)) %>%
    ungroup() %>%
    group_by(participant_id, trial) %>%
    mutate(gaze_outlier = identify_gaze_outliers(gaze_x, gaze_y)) %>%
    ungroup() %>%
    filter(!(rt_outlier %in% TRUE), !gaze_outlier) %>%
    select(-rt_outlier, -gaze_outlier)

  # Areas of interest (the solvable/nonsolvable boxes follow the solvable side).
  combined <- combined %>%
    mutate(Trial = Target) %>%
    add_aoi(aoi_box_solvable, "gaze_x", "gaze_y", "Solvable", "Left", "Right", "Top", "Bottom") %>%
    add_aoi(aoi_box_nonsolvable, "gaze_x", "gaze_y", "Nonsolvable", "Left", "Right", "Top", "Bottom") %>%
    select(-Trial)

  # eyetrackingR object, response window, and track-loss-based exclusion.
  item_cols <- if (has_contrast) c("affect", "contrast") else "affect"
  et <- make_eyetrackingr_data(
    combined,
    participant_column = "participant_id", trial_column = "trial",
    item_columns = item_cols, time_column = "time_from_onset",
    trackloss_column = "trackloss", aoi_columns = c("Solvable", "Nonsolvable"),
    treat_non_aoi_looks_as_missing = FALSE
  )
  et <- subset_by_window(et, window_start_time = 0, window_end_time = 10, remove = TRUE)
  trackloss <- trackloss_analysis(et)
  et <- clean_by_trackloss(et, trial_prop_thresh = track_exclude_prop,
                           participant_prop_thresh = track_exclude_prop)

  list(data = et, trackloss = trackloss, n_joined = n_joined)
}

title: Data pipeline and dictionary
text: How raw records become analysis-ready datasets, and what every field means. The pipeline has three stages: extract (Python) → preprocess (analysis/01_preprocessing.qmd) → analyse (analysis/02–04).

title: Data pipeline and dictionary
text:
1 Task
Each trial shows two triads of words side by side. One triad is solvable (its three words share a remote associate, e.g. woda · płuca · kamień → kamień-themed); the other is nonsolvable. The participant picks the solvable triad (keys q/p = left/right), rates confidence (0–10), then guesses the associate. Study 1 manipulates the solvable triad’s affective valence (Negative/Neutral/Positive); Study 2 additionally manipulates contrast (which triad is shown in high-contrast black vs. low-contrast grey).

title: Data pipeline and dictionary
text:
2 Stage 1 — extract (scripts/extract_data.py)
Reads the raw records directly and labels gaze with trials. Intent: turn per-session iohub samples + the PsychoPy behavioral log into tidy, per-trial tables, keyed consistently by participant.
Inputs: - data/raw/eyetracking/exp{1,2*}.hdf5 — iohub HDF5. Uses BinocularEyeSampleEvent (per-eye gaze in PsychoPy centred pixels, status, pupil — pupil unused), MessageEvent (start:<id> / end:<id> trial markers; validation = calibration check), and session_meta_data (session_id → participant name). - data/raw/behavioral/exp{1,2}/…csv — one PsychoPy log per participant.
Extraction rules: - Participant id = the filename code (zero-padded), which matches the iohub session name. The CSV participant field is unreliable and is not used. - Confidence = the integer 0–10 in ocena_1.text (decision confidence). The textbox is noisy in Study 2 (stray keystrokes), so the embedded digit is extracted; trials without one are missing. - acc = 9 (no response in the 10 s window) → accuracy/RT/confidence missing. - Each validation marker starts a new block (run); Stage 2 resolves restarts by keeping each participant’s last block.
Outputs (data/processed/): - labelled/exp{1,2}.csv — one row per gaze sample: participant_id, [condition,] block, trial, event,   time, left/right_gaze_x/y, status. - behavioral/exp{1,2}.csv — one row per trial: experiment_id, participant_id, [condition,] block, trial,   event, triad_solvable, affect, side_solve, [side_contrast,] accuracy, accuracy_rt, confidence, solution,   sex, age. - stimuli.csv — one row per triad: experiment_id, code, role (solvable/nonsolvable), affect, word_1..3.

title: Data pipeline and dictionary
text:
3 Stage 2 — preprocess (analysis/01_preprocessing.qmd)
Intent: join the two streams, build clean gaze with areas of interest, and exclude poor-quality data.

Combine gaze + behavioral on (participant, [condition,] trial, event), keeping each participant’s last block.
Binocular gaze (compute_binocular_gaze): average both eyes when valid, else the single valid eye, else track loss — an eye is valid when within the screen ± 10%. Transform to screen pixels.
Interpolate gaps ≤ 100 ms; longer gaps stay track loss.
Outliers: RT beyond 1.5 × IQR (per participant), gaze beyond the 97.5th Mahalanobis percentile (per trial).
AOIs: 400 × 300 px boxes over each triad (x ∈ [310,710]/[1210,1610], y ∈ [390,690]), following the solvable side; restrict to the 0–10 s window; exclude trials and participants with > 40% track loss.

Output: data/processed/prepared/exp{1,2}.Rds — an eyetrackingR object (analysed N = 39 / 45).

title: Data pipeline and dictionary
text:
4 Stage 3 — analyse (analysis/02–04)

02_study1.qmd, 03_study2.qmd — accuracy (binomial), RT (log-Gaussian), confidence (Gaussian), and gaze preference (growth-curve analysis); Type III omnibus tests, FDR contrasts, effect sizes.
04_robustness.qmd — stimulus norming + covariate confound test, sex moderation, cross-study RT, equivalence tests for the Study 2 nulls, simulation-based power.

Preference score (per time bin): (looks_Solvable − looks_Nonsolvable) / (looks_Solvable + looks_Nonsolvable); samples outside both AOIs are excluded from numerator and denominator.

title: Data pipeline and dictionary
text:
5 Note on validity
The pipeline applies the track-loss exclusions described above; two Study 2 participants with essentially no valid gaze are excluded, so the analysed samples are N = 39 (Study 1) and N = 45 (Study 2). Stimulus-side robustness checks (norming-based covariate adjustment of the valence effects) are reported in analysis/04_robustness.qmd.
